claim: Taxis behaviour in Drosophila larva is thought to consist of distinct control mechanisms triggering specific actions.
source: Taxis behaviour in Drosophila larva is thought to consist of distinct control mechanisms triggering specific actions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background context for the study.

claim: Larvae display a rhythmic, continuous lateral oscillation of the anterior body, encompassing all head-sweeps, small or large, without breaking the oscillatory rhythm.
source: Our analysis of larvae motion reveals a rhythmic, continuous lateral oscillation of the anterior body, encompassing all head-sweeps, small or large, without breaking the oscillatory rhythm.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of larval motion data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: An agent-model that embeds the hypothesis of continuous lateral oscillation reproduces a surprising number of taxis signatures observed in larvae.
source: Further, we show that an agent-model that embeds this hypothesis reproduces a surprising number of taxis signatures observed in larvae.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figures 3-7.

claim: By coupling the sensory input to a neural oscillator in continuous time, the mechanism is robust and biologically plausible.
source: Also, by coupling the sensory input to a neural oscillator in continuous time, we show that the mechanism is robust and biologically plausible.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the continuous-time neural model presented in Figure 8.

claim: The mechanism provides a simple architecture for combining information across modalities.
source: The mechanism provides a simple architecture for combining information across modalities, and explaining how learnt associations modulate taxis.
evidence: This is discussed conceptually in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 9C.

claim: Larvae of Drosophila display taxis behaviours by spontaneously crawling towards or away from the source of stimuli such as odours.
source: The larvae of Drosophila display taxis behaviours by spontaneously crawling towards or away from the source of stimuli such as odours, or more generally, up or down stimulus gradients, including chemical, light and temperature gradients (Luo et al., 2010; Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012; Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2014; Kane et al., 2013; Klein et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Larval taxis behaviour is flexible and can be altered by associative learning if the stimulus is presented together with a positive or negative reinforcer.
source: This behavioural tendency is flexible and can be altered by associative learning if the stimulus is presented together with a positive or negative reinforcer (Scherer et al., 2003; Gerber et al., 2004; Ache and Young, 2005; Diegelmann et al., 2013; Schleyer et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on associative learning in larvae.

claim: The main chemosensory organ is located on the head of Drosophila larvae.
source: The main chemosensory organ is located on the head, and the small spatial separation of the bilateral olfactory receptors makes it unlikely that the animal can detect the instantaneous odour gradient.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about larval anatomy.

claim: The small spatial separation of the bilateral olfactory receptors makes it unlikely that the larva can detect the instantaneous odour gradient.
source: The main chemosensory organ is located on the head, and the small spatial separation of the bilateral olfactory receptors makes it unlikely that the animal can detect the instantaneous odour gradient.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical constraints of the larval sensory system.

claim: Larvae can still chemotax with a single active receptor.
source: In fact, it has been shown that larvae can still chemotax with a single active receptor (Fishilevich et al., 2005; Gomez-Marin et al., 2010; Louis et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: The key information used by the larva appears to be the change in odour concentration experienced as it moves forward and/or casts its head sideways.
source: The key information used by the larva appears to be the change in odour concentration experienced as it moves forward and/or casts its head sideways (Gomez-Marin et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Olfactory sensory neurons give strong transient responses during changes in odour concentration.
source: Olfactory sensory neurons are well suited to carry this information as they have been shown to give strong transient responses during changes in odour concentration (De Palo et al., 2013; Nagel and Wilson, 2011; Kim et al., 2011; Schulze et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The frequency and direction of turns appears correlated to decreases or increases in the perceived concentration.
source: and the frequency and direction of turns (large body bends leading to a new trajectory direction) appears correlated to decreases or increases in the perceived concentration (Hernandez-Nunez et al., 2015; Schulze et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Recent studies reveal substantial similarity in the characteristics of larval taxis behaviour across different modalities.
source: but recent studies reveal substantial similarity in the characteristics of larval taxis behaviour across different modalities (Gepner et al., 2015; Bellmann et al., 2010; Lahiri et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Several models have been designed to capture quantitatively the observed larval behaviour during its approach to an odour source.
source: Several models have been designed to capture quantitatively the observed larval behaviour during its approach to an odour source (Davies et al., 2015; Hernandez-Nunez et al., 2015; Schleyer et al., 2015a; Gepner et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: Previous models typically assume the expression of taxis consists of multiple behavioural states with state transitions that are biased by sensory stimuli.
source: These models typically assume the expression of taxis consists of multiple behavioural states with state transitions that are biased by sensory stimuli.
evidence: This is a characterization of prior modeling approaches.

claim: The Davies et al. (2015) model reproduces many characteristics of larval chemotaxis by combining three mechanisms: biased forward runs (weathervaning), increased probability to stop runs when odour concentration decreases (klinokinesis), and increased probability to resume running when a head cast is in a direction that increases the experienced odour concentration (klinotaxis).
source: In Davies et al. (2015); a model closely based on the behavioural analyses in Lahiri et al. (2011); Gomez-Marin and Louis (2014); Gomez-Marin et al. (2011); Ohashi et al. (2014) reproduces many characteristics of larval chemotaxis by combining three mechanisms: biased forward runs (weathervaning), increased probability to stop runs when odour concentration decreases (klinokinesis), and increased probability to resume running when a head cast is in a direction that increases the experienced odour concentration (klinotaxis).
evidence: This describes the mechanisms in a prior model with citations.

claim: Behavioural observation shows rather strong similarities in the behavioural modulations resulting from apparently unrelated conditions, such as odour-tastant associative learning and variation of stimulus concentration.
source: However, behavioural observation shows rather strong similarities in the behavioural modulations resulting from apparently unrelated conditions, such as odour-tastant associative learning and variation of stimulus concentration (Schleyer et al., 2015a)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: A recent attempt to categorise larval behavioural states using an unsupervised method based on the animal's posture suggests the existence of a continuum rather than clear-cut categories.
source: Also, a recent attempt to categorise larval behavioural states using an unsupervised method based on the animal's posture suggests the existence of a continuum rather than clear-cut categories (Szigeti et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Closed-loop sensory modulation of an intrinsic motor pattern can be a particularly efficient neural mechanism for flexible behavioural control.
source: Specifically, inspired by the description in larvae of frequent low amplitude head sweeps, which modulate run direction (Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2014), and the idea that closed-loop sensory modulation of an intrinsic motor pattern can be a particularly efficient neural mechanism for flexible behavioural control (Izquierdo and Lockery, 2010; Kanzaki, 1996; Levi et al., 2005; Willis and Arbas, 1997b)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on motor control mechanisms.

claim: Larvae display frequent low amplitude head sweeps, which modulate run direction.
source: Specifically, inspired by the description in larvae of frequent low amplitude head sweeps, which modulate run direction (Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The analysis reveals that larvae display continuous anterior body oscillation.
source: Our analysis reveals that larvae indeed display continuous anterior body oscillation.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Direct sensory modulation of oscillation amplitude is sufficient to reproduce many specific larval taxis signatures, without requiring specific parameter tuning to different conditions.
source: We show, in both a simple discrete-time model and a neural model in continuous time, that direct sensory modulation of oscillation amplitude is sufficient to reproduce many specific larval taxis signatures, without requiring specific parameter tuning to different conditions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the modeling results presented in Figures 3-8.

claim: 42 wild-type larvae performing innate chemotaxis were analyzed.
source: We used previously recorded tracks of 42 wild-type larvae performing innate chemotaxis (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011) to analyse the body-bend, the anterior body angular velocity and the forward speed.
evidence: This describes the data source used for analysis.

claim: The analysis reveals a continuous alternation between left and right turns, which appears most clearly in the angular velocity of the anterior part of the body.
source: This reveals a continuous alternation between left and right turns, which appears most clearly in the angular velocity of the anterior part of the body (Figure 1A 'blue line').
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Larvae regularly stop their forward peristalsis motion and display large lateral head sweeps.
source: Larvae are known to regularly stop their forward peristalsis motion and display large lateral head sweeps (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as known behavior with citation.

claim: Head sweeps do not break the continuous alternation between left and right turns.
source: A closer look shows that these head sweeps do not seem to break the continuous alternation between left and right turns, i.e., if the larva's head was moving left before stopping the peristalsis motion, the first head sweep after stopping will be to the right, and vice versa (Figure 1B and Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 1B and 2A,B.

claim: Head sweeps appear to be part of a continuous oscillation rather than individual motor actions triggered independently.
source: Thus, these head sweeps appear to be part of a continuous oscillation rather than individual motor actions triggered independently.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that head sweeps maintain the oscillatory pattern.

claim: The distribution of body bending, anterior body angular velocity and acceleration, as well as the extent of each lateral oscillation of the anterior body, show a smooth curve with no signs of bimodality.
source: Also, the distribution of body bending, anterior body angular velocity and acceleration, as well as the extent of each lateral oscillation of the anterior body, show a smooth curve with no signs of bimodality (Figure 2D) suggesting a continuum of turning modulation rather than a discrete set of distinguishable actions.
evidence: This is supported by the distributions shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The smooth distributions suggest a continuum of turning modulation rather than a discrete set of distinguishable actions.
source: Also, the distribution of body bending, anterior body angular velocity and acceleration, as well as the extent of each lateral oscillation of the anterior body, show a smooth curve with no signs of bimodality (Figure 2D) suggesting a continuum of turning modulation rather than a discrete set of distinguishable actions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the smooth distributions observed in Figure 2D.

claim: A Fourier analysis confirms the existence of an oscillatory rhythm with a mean frequency around 0.3 Hz.
source: A Fourier analysis confirms the existence of an oscillatory rhythm with a mean frequency around 0.3 Hz; that is roughly one turn left and one turn right every 3.3 s (Figure 2C, blue).
evidence: This is supported by the Fourier analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The turning oscillation seems decoupled from the peristalsis motion.
source: This turning oscillation seems decoupled from the peristalsis motion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which operates around a mean frequency of 1.1 Hz (Figure 2C, green).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2C.

claim: The peristalsis rhythm operates around a mean frequency of 1.1 Hz.
source: This turning oscillation seems decoupled from the peristalsis motion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which operates around a mean frequency of 1.1 Hz (Figure 2C, green).
evidence: This is supported by the Fourier analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The peristalsis rhythm appears remarkably constant, perhaps because of biomechanical constraints.
source: The peristalsis rhythm appears remarkably constant, perhaps because of biomechanical constraints (Ross et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an observation with a speculative explanation supported by citation.

claim: A direct coupling between peristalsis and turning oscillation would constrain the larvae to spend as much time sweeping left as sweeping right, which would restrict the flexibility in trajectory alterations.
source: Therefore, a direct coupling between peristalsis and turning oscillation would constrain the larvae to spend as much time sweeping left as sweeping right, which would restrict the flexibility in trajectory alterations.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of coupling the two rhythms.

claim: By having the lateral oscillations decoupled from peristalsis, the relative duration between left and right sweeps can vary.
source: By having the lateral oscillations decoupled from peristalsis, however, the relative duration between left and right sweeps can vary.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the advantage of decoupling.

claim: A curving path to the left is achieved by spending slightly more time (and also increasing the angular speed of the head sweep) sweeping left than sweeping right.
source: This is indeed what we observed in larvae. A curving path to the left for instance, is achieved by spending slightly more time (and also increasing the angular speed of the head sweep) sweeping left than sweeping right (Figure 1A 'blue region': Time spent turning right = 12.9 s; Time spent turning left = 22.9 s; Ratio right/left = 0.64. Integral left = 179.3 degrees; Integral right = −64.6 degrees; Total = 114.7 degrees left; Ratio right/left = 0.73).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis of the path shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Larvae show larger and quicker head sweeps when the peristalsis motion has stopped.
source: Even-though larvae show larger and quicker head sweeps when the peristalsis motion has stopped (Figure 2F), the head sweep duration is similar between crawling phases and stop phases (Figure 2E), suggesting again the existence of a shared underlying oscillatory rhythm.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: The head sweep duration is similar between crawling phases and stop phases, suggesting the existence of a shared underlying oscillatory rhythm.
source: Even-though larvae show larger and quicker head sweeps when the peristalsis motion has stopped (Figure 2F), the head sweep duration is similar between crawling phases and stop phases (Figure 2E), suggesting again the existence of a shared underlying oscillatory rhythm.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the similarity in head sweep durations shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A continuous lateral oscillation of the anterior body sits at the core of the chemotaxis mechanism.
source: To summarise, our observations support the hypothesis that a continuous lateral oscillation of the anterior body sits at the core of the chemotaxis mechanism, and that its rhythm is decoupled to the peristaltic rhythm thus allowing more freedom to adjust the head-turning velocity and amplitude.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: The rhythm of the lateral oscillation is decoupled to the peristaltic rhythm thus allowing more freedom to adjust the head-turning velocity and amplitude.
source: To summarise, our observations support the hypothesis that a continuous lateral oscillation of the anterior body sits at the core of the chemotaxis mechanism, and that its rhythm is decoupled to the peristaltic rhythm thus allowing more freedom to adjust the head-turning velocity and amplitude.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the data analysis and logical inference.

claim: The simple oscillatory agent reproduces taxis.
source: Figure 3C,D shows that this simple agent is sufficient for taxis to emerge.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: For an attractive odour, the distribution of bearing angle to the odour's source shows two peaks around 90 and −90 degrees in the agent model.
source: An emergent property of our agent model is that for an attractive odour (i.e. a negative gain) the distribution of bearing angle to the odour's source shows two peaks around 90 and −90 degrees (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 4.

claim: The agent tends to spend more time with the odour on its sides rather than directly in front or behind it.
source: Therefore, the agent tends to spend more time with the odour on its sides rather than directly in front or behind it.
evidence: This is an inference from the bearing angle distribution.

claim: Real larvae also tend to spend more time with the odour on their sides.
source: Interestingly, this is also true with real larvae (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in the larval data in Figure 4.

claim: For both larvae and simulated agents, orbital behaviour is emphasized during peristalsis forward motion.
source: In both larvae and simulation, orbital behaviour is emphasized during peristalsis forward motion (turn < 30 degrees for the model) (C blue curve), and when the larvae/agent is more than 1cm away from the odour (D green curve).
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Crossing-over trajectories are constituted of regular large turns that happen mostly while the larvae/agent is heading away from the odour.
source: Crossing-over trajectories, by contrast, are constituted of regular large turns that happen mostly while the larvae/agent is heading away from the odour (C red curve) and is rather apparent when the larvae/agent is close to the odour (D blue curve).
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Spending time with the odour located 90 degrees on the side translates into orbiting around the odour source.
source: Spending time with the odour located 90 degrees on the side translates into orbiting around the odour source.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the bearing angle distribution.

claim: Orbital behaviour can be observed clearly in simulated trajectories from the deterministic version of the agent model.
source: This 'orbital behaviour' can be observed clearly in simulated trajectories from the deterministic (absence of random noise) version of our agent model (Figures 4B and 5B).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figures 4B and 5B.

claim: Increasing the gain results in a qualitative change to the shape of agent's trajectories from circular orbits to those characterized by straight crossings over the odour source.
source: However, in our models, increasing the gain (towards higher negative values) results in a qualitative change to the shape of agent's trajectories from circular orbits to those characterized by straight crossings over the odour source, and sharp re-orientation events once the peak has been passed over, that is, when the odour source is now located behind the agent (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 4B.

claim: Examination of actual larvae paths reveals similar signature: crossing-over trajectories emerge when close to the odour source.
source: Examination of actual larvae paths reveals similar signature: crossing-over trajectories emerge when close to the odour source [except for the Or42a single receptor mutant larvae, that show an orbital behaviour (see below)], which indeed results in a flattening of the distribution curve (Figure 4A,D).
evidence: This is shown in the larval data in Figure 4A,D.

claim: Genetic alterations of the peripheral olfactory circuits that reduce the number of functional OSNs increase the spread of trajectories around a source.
source: For instance, genetic alterations of the peripheral olfactory circuits that reduce the number of functional OSNs (Louis et al., 2008; Gomez-Marin et al., 2011) or receptor diversity (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011) increase the spread of trajectories around a source, and can produce trajectories that seem to maintain a distance from the source (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: As the gain is reduced, the spread of trajectories increases, and orbital trajectories eventually arise.
source: As the gain is reduced, the spread of trajectories increases, and orbital trajectories eventually arise: the agent maintains a radial distance from the source.
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 5B.

claim: Schleyer et al. (2015b) describe in detail the effects of changing the concentration of the odour source on the statistics of larval chemotaxis.
source: Schleyer et al. (2015b) describe in detail the effects of changing the concentration of the odour source on the statistics of larval chemotaxis.
evidence: This is a citation to prior research.

claim: Similar behavioural effects are obtained after associative learning as after changing odour concentration.
source: Perhaps surprisingly, they show that similar behavioural effects are obtained after associative learning (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in the data from Schleyer et al. (2015b) presented in Figure 5C.

claim: In the model, the performance index increases quite linearly with change in gain.
source: In our model, the performance index increases quite linearly with change in gain (Figure 5E)
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 5E.

claim: The model can account for the continuum of performance indices observed in larvae across experiments.
source: and can therefore account for the continuum of performance indices observed in larvae across experiments.
evidence: This is an inference from the linear relationship between gain and performance index.

claim: In previous agent simulation models, small changes in parameter values would yield drastic changes in performance index.
source: This was not necessarily the case in previous agent simulation models, where small changes in parameter values would yield drastic changes in performance index (Davies et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior modeling work with citation.

claim: The average sensory history perceived before the occurrence of large turns shows a slow monotonic decrease in concentration which extends up to 10s prior to the large turn.
source: The average sensory history perceived before the occurrence of large turns shows a slow monotonic decrease in concentration which extends up to 10s prior to the large turn. This has been reported for larvae during chemotaxis (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011) or as a response to white noise optogenetic stimulation of olfactory receptor (Gepner et al., 2015), and can also be observed in our model (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in the model results in Figure 6.

claim: The model does not possess a low-pass filter: large turns occur as the consequence of the stimulus change perceived during the last time-step only.
source: However, our model does not possess such a low-pass filter: large turns occur as the consequence of the stimulus change perceived during the last time-step only.
evidence: This is a statement about the model structure.

claim: The monotonic sensory decrease can result from the structure of the environment, and not from a low-pass filter in the larva.
source: Therefore, the monotonic sensory decrease can result from the structure of the environment, and not from a low-pass filter in the larva.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: Larvae show a slight tendency to bias their first head cast (after a stop event) towards the side of the attractive stimulus.
source: Larvae show a slight tendency to bias their first head cast (after a stop event) towards the side of the attractive stimulus (i.e. the odour side (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012) or darker side during negative phototaxis (Kane et al., 2013), or towards preferred temperatures (Luo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The agent model also reveals a tendency to bias its first 'turns' towards the odour source.
source: But if we identify 'turns' in our model as those re-orientation angles exceeding the threshold that is usually associated with stopping in the larva, the agent also reveals a tendency to bias its first 'turns' towards the odour source (Figure 7), despite having no gradient information other than the change from one time step to the next.
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 7.

claim: The first-turn bias arises because of the oscillatory nature of the agent.
source: This tendency arises because of the oscillatory nature of the agent.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism.

claim: The model predicts that the first-turn bias should increase together with increasing odour attraction.
source: Our model predicts that the bias should increase together with increasing odour attraction, whether from stronger gain due to appetitive learning; stronger sensory input due to increased odour concentration, or both (Figure 7A)
evidence: This is a prediction from the model shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The first-turn bias should become more apparent when the odour is located on one side of the larvae.
source: it should also become more apparent when the odour is located on one side of the larvae (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The discrete-time sensorimotor model assumed that head-sweeps and sensory perception are instantaneous and synchronized.
source: The discrete-time sensorimotor model assumed that head-sweeps and sensory perception are instantaneous and synchronized, which might imply that the descending sensory signal in the larvae may require precise timing in order to interact with the ongoing motor control of the oscillation.
evidence: This is a statement about the assumptions of the discrete-time model.

claim: The continuous-time model aims to investigate whether the hypothesis can be verified in continuous time given the biophysical constraints of a neural implementation.
source: Here, we aim to investigate whether our hypothesis can be verified in continuous time given the biophysical constraints of a neural implementation.
evidence: This is a statement of the purpose of the continuous-time model.

claim: The change in heading is driven by a neural oscillator in continuous time in the continuous-time model.
source: The agent is again abstracted to an oriented point-sensor but now, critically, the change in heading is driven by a neural oscillator in continuous time, while sensory stimuli are continuously updated under the agent's motion through the environment.
evidence: This is a description of the continuous-time model structure.

claim: The CPG model was adapted from a spike-rate neural model that has been successfully used to model lamprey locomotion.
source: For our purposes, we adapted (see 'Materials and methods' ) a spike-rate neural model of a central pattern generator (CPG) that has been successfully used to model lamprey locomotion (Cohen et al., 1992; Lansner and Griller, 1997) see Marder and Calabrese, 1996.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: The CPG consists of a pair of compartments driving the changes in the agent's heading.
source: The CPG consists of a pair of compartments, here taken to be driving the changes in the agent's heading (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a description of the CPG model structure shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In the absence of stimuli, the CPG parameters have been set to produce a regular ±10 degrees oscillation in the heading at around 0.3 Hz.
source: In the absence of stimuli arriving from the input unit A, the parameters of the system have been set so that it produces a regular ±10 degrees oscillation in the heading at around 0.3 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the model parameters.

claim: The sensory input allows the oscillation to be perturbed, modifying the amplitude and phase relationships between the bursts of each side, resulting in a change in the agent's heading.
source: The sensory input allows this oscillation to be perturbed, modifying the amplitude and phase relationships between the bursts of each side, resulting in a change in the agent's heading.
evidence: This is a description of how sensory input affects the CPG model.

claim: The resulting steering varied smoothly across the oscillator phase and therefore it is not critically dependent on the precise timing of the perturbation.
source: The resulting steering varied smoothly across the oscillator phase and therefore it is not critically dependent on the precise timing of the perturbation (see Figure 8F).
evidence: This is shown in the analysis in Figure 8F.

claim: The continuous agent produces curved paths when further away from the odour source, characteristic of larval behaviour, that subsequently become orbits around the odour source.
source: In a virtual odour environment, the continuous agent also produces curved paths when further away from the odour source, characteristic of larval behaviour, that subsequently become orbits around the odour source (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 8D.

claim: The frequency of oscillation in the continuous-time model is within the ranges observed in larva.
source: The parameters of the model have been set such that the frequency of oscillation is within the ranges observed in larva (see Figure 8C)
evidence: This is shown in the frequency spectrum in Figure 8C.

claim: The heading velocity dynamics emerging from the continuous-time model are reminiscent of the experimental data of anterior body angular velocity.
source: The heading velocity dynamics emerging from the model (Figure 8E) are reminiscent of the experimental data of anterior body angular velocity (Figure 1) in terms that in both there is a baseline rhythm while heading velocity increases under larger re-orientations (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is a comparison between the model results in Figure 8E and the larval data in Figure 1.

claim: Rhythmic behaviour is ubiquitous in biological systems.
source: Rhythmic behaviour is ubiquitous in biological systems.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge.

claim: Producing oscillations during locomotion is widespread in biological systems, from multisegmented animals down to single cells.
source: Producing oscillations during locomotion is widespread in biological systems, from multisegmented animals (Iino and Yoshida, 2009; Izquierdo and Lockery, 2010; Lansner and Griller, 1997) down to single cells (Yang et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Oscillations may have advantages for sensorimotor control when tracking up an odour trail or plume.
source: and may have advantages for sensorimotor control when tracking up an odour trail or plume (Hangartner, 1969; Farkas and Shorey, 1972; Budick and Dickinson, 2006; Willis and Arbas, 1997a; Cardé and Willis, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Larval taxis behaviour has been characterised as transitions between discrete states, or actions.
source: Larval taxis behaviour has been characterised as transitions between discrete states, or actions (Green et al., 1983; Sawin et al., 1994; Cobb, 1999; Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012) requiring 'action-selection' or 'decision-making' processes (Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Running/weathervaning and casting/turning all result from the same underlying and continuously active oscillatory mechanism.
source: That is, we suggest running/weathervaning and casting/turning all result from the same underlying and continuously active oscillatory mechanism (Figure 9C,D), and that taxis involves continuous and direct sensory modulation of the oscillation amplitude.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the paper, illustrated in Figure 9C,D.

claim: Models embodying the oscillatory hypothesis, despite their simplicity, are sufficient to capture a range of taxis phenomena observed in larvae.
source: We show that models embodying this hypothesis, despite their simplicity, are sufficient to capture a range of taxis phenomena observed in larvae (Figures 4, 5, 7, 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the modeling results in Figures 4, 5, 7, 8.

claim: In the oscillatory taxis mechanism, 'directed' motion by the animal towards a target does not require a lateralised descending signal.
source: In this oscillatory taxis mechanism, 'directed' motion by the animal towards a target does not require a lateralised descending signal, nor does it include any switch between states or actions.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of the proposed mechanism.

claim: Robust steering emerges from the closed-loop nature of the system.
source: Robust steering simply emerges from the closed-loop nature of the system: the oscillations control the exposure of the sensor to the stimuli, and the sensory signal controls the oscillations by perturbing the stable cyclic dynamics of the oscillator.
evidence: This is an explanation of how the mechanism works.

claim: A CPG is believed to operate within the thoracic and abdominal segments of larvae, executing a motor program for exploratory locomotion.
source: A CPG is believed to operate within the thoracic and abdominal segments of larvae, executing a motor program for exploratory locomotion (Hughes and Thomas, 2007; Berni et al., 2012; Lemon et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A recurrent CPG circuit generating oscillations is consistent with cross-connections in the ventral nerve cord of the larva.
source: while a recurrent CPG circuit generating oscillations is consistent with cross-connections in the ventral nerve cord of the larva (Kohsaka et al., 2012; Rickert et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Genetic disruption of the mid-line connection pattern, particularly in the anterior segments (T1, T2, T3), disrupts lateral body bending.
source: Indeed, genetic disruption of the mid-line connection pattern, particularly in the anterior segments (T1, T2, T3), disrupts lateral body bending (Berni, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The key mapping underlying taxis behaviour is a direct relationship of the perceived sensory signal to the modulation of oscillation amplitude.
source: We propose that the key mapping underlying taxis behaviour is a direct relationship of the perceived sensory signal to the modulation of oscillation amplitude.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism.

claim: The gain could be seen as the net effect of the complete pathway from the stimulation of sensory receptors to muscle contraction.
source: Rather, it could be seen as the net effect of the complete pathway from the stimulation of sensory receptors to muscle contraction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the model parameter represents biologically.

claim: A single degree of freedom is sufficient to capture a substantial range of characteristics of the animal's behaviour.
source: However, the fact that a single degree of freedom is sufficient to capture a substantial range of characteristics of the animal's behaviour, including the path signatures (Figures 4) as well as the effect of odour-tastant associations, or reductions in the number of ORs (Figure 5) can be informative for reconstructing the neural architecture underlying chemotaxis in larvae.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: All parallel sensory pathways simply need to converge and sum their signals.
source: All parallel sensory pathways simply need to converge and sum their signals (Figure 9C), whether inhibitory or excitatory.
evidence: This is a proposed architecture illustrated in Figure 9C.

claim: The net sum of converged signals will determine the valence (attraction or repulsion) and the strength of the chemotactic response.
source: The net sum will determine the valence (attraction or repulsion) and the strength of the chemotactic response.
evidence: This is an inference from the proposed architecture.

claim: Associative learning is believed to be based on experience-driven plasticity of the mushroom body (MB) pathway.
source: For example, associative learning is believed to be based on experience-driven plasticity of the mushroom body (MB) pathway (Gerber et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Learning is seen as a change in the effective signal transmission of the MB pathway, which runs parallel to the innate one, before both converge onto the motor system.
source: and here learning is seen as a change in the effective signal transmission of this pathway, which runs parallel to the innate one, before both converge onto the motor system.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of how learning affects the system.

claim: The proposed mechanism is consistent with the results of Schleyer et al. (2015a) showing that learning and changes in odour concentration yield similar motor effects.
source: This is consistent with the results of Schleyer et al. (2015a) showing that learning and changes in odour concentration yield similar motor effects
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The proposed mechanism is consistent with the results of Gepner et al. (2015) suggesting that larvae combine olfactory and visual signals upstream of the decision to turn.
source: as well as the results of Gepner et al. (2015) suggesting that larvae combine olfactory and visual signals upstream of the decision to turn.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The proposed mechanism explains the apparent similarity of taxis behaviours observed across modalities.
source: It also explains the apparent similarity of taxis behaviours observed across modalities (compare for odour: Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; light: Kane et al., 2013, temperature: Lahiri et al., 2011
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research across different modalities.

claim: When aversive light stimulus and attractive olfactory stimulation are perfectly synchronized their antagonistic effects appear to blend smoothly.
source: and why when aversive light stimulus and attractive olfactory stimulation are perfectly synchronized their antagonistic effects appear to blend smoothly (see Bellmann et al., 2010, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: A state-based model needs to postulate that all factors have equivalent and parallel effects on multiple mechanisms to account for the observed results.
source: A state-based model, by contrast, needs to postulate that all these factors have equivalent and parallel effects on multiple mechanisms to account for these results (Davies et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison to alternative models with citation.

claim: Peristalsis inhibition is not crucial for the emergence of the taxis signatures discussed.
source: The models' results show that peristalsis inhibition is not crucial for the emergence of the taxis signatures discussed above.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: Crawling speed in larvae can be reduced down to zero, and this is correlated with large body bends.
source: However, it is clear that crawling speed in larvae can be reduced down to zero, and this is correlated with large body bends (Figure 1 tail speed), and thus has an impact on chemotaxis behaviour.
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 1.

claim: The inhibition of the forward motion is triggered on average at the onset of the turn and is thus not a mere consequence of large body bends.
source: However, our analysis (consistent with Gepner et al., 2015; Hernandez-Nunez et al., 2015) shows that the inhibition of the forward motion is triggered on average at the onset of the turn and is thus not a mere consequence of large body bends (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is shown in the analysis in Figure 9B and supported by citations.

claim: Speed reduction is graded.
source: We also note from our analysis that speed reduction is graded (Figure 1B,C)
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The tail speed distribution is bimodal.
source: although contrary to turning amplitude (Figure 2D), the tail speed distribution is bimodal (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is shown in the data in Figure 9A.

claim: The same signal that changes the oscillation amplitude could also directly change the peristalsis speed.
source: Our simple suggestion, then, is that the same signal that changes the oscillation amplitude could also directly change the peristalsis speed, which below some threshold results in a stop.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism.

claim: Average speed, frequency of stopping events and average body-bending amplitude co-vary across stimuli conditions.
source: There is some experimental data suggesting that average speed, frequency of stopping events and average body-bending amplitude co-vary across stimuli conditions.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of experimental observations.

claim: Larva both reduce their crawling speed and increase their turn-rate in response to large step increases in CO2.
source: Larva both reduce their crawling speed and increase their turn-rate in response to large step increases in CO2 (Gershow et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Larvae tend to accelerate when moving up a chemical gradient which is correlated with a reduced turn-rate.
source: Larvae tend to accelerate when moving up a chemical gradient (Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2014) which is correlated with a reduced turn-rate (Schleyer et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Fast escape responses involve reduced head sweeping and rapid crawling.
source: Fast escape responses involve reduced head sweeping and rapid crawling (Ohyama et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The oscillator hypothesis predicts that all head-sweeps are under the control of the same oscillator, independently if the animal has stopped or is running.
source: We have assumed that all head-sweeps are under the control of the same oscillator, independently if the animal has stopped or is running.
evidence: This is a stated assumption that leads to predictions.

claim: The head-sweep amplitude should decrease under favourable changes, such as moving up-gradient towards an attractive odour, and increase under unfavourable changes.
source: The head-sweep amplitude should decrease under favourable changes, such as moving up-gradient towards an attractive odour, and increase under unfavourable changes.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: 'Stop and head-cast' events should be preceded by a smaller head-sweep in the opposite direction.
source: It also follows that 'stop and head-cast' events should be preceded by a smaller head-sweep in the opposite direction, which indeed agrees with our analysis of larval tracks in (Figures 1B and 2A,B), whatever the conditions.
evidence: This is a prediction that is supported by the data in Figures 1B and 2A,B.

claim: 'Stop and head-cast' and 'weathervaning' behaviours are not independent mechanisms.
source: This relationship implies that 'stop and head-cast' and 'weathervaning' behaviours are not independent mechanisms, and hence, for example, it should not be possible to obtain neurogenetic control over one without affecting the other.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: The oscillator hypothesis predicts that stimulus elicited responses are timing dependent.
source: The oscillator hypothesis predicts that stimulus elicited responses are timing dependent.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: The continuous model predicts that experimentally varying the timing of stimulus exposure would trigger head-sweeps whose magnitude and direction vary as a function of the state of the oscillator at the time of stimulation.
source: Specifically, the continuous model predicts that experimentally varying the timing of stimulus exposure, for example via optogenetically induced olfactory stimulation, would trigger head-sweeps whose magnitude and direction vary as a function of the state of the oscillator at the time of stimulation.
evidence: This is a prediction from the continuous-time model.

claim: A state-based model would predict that a step stimulus during re-orientation could trigger a termination of the head-sweep and a transition to the run state.
source: In contrast, a state-based model would predict that a step stimulus during re-orientation could trigger a termination of the head-sweep and a transition to the run state, thus 'accepting' a new heading direction.
evidence: This is a contrasting prediction from alternative models.

claim: Current theory supports the view that memory expression is due to efficacy changes in synapses converging to mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) that encode valence.
source: Current theory supports the view that memory expression is due to efficacy changes in synapses converging to mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) that encode valence; stimulating these neurons can elicit attraction or aversion (Aso et al., 2014; Sachse and Beshel, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The model suggests that the mushroom body pathway is yet another pathway that converges to modify the effective gain in the motor system.
source: However, our model suggests that the mushroom body pathway is yet another pathway that converges to modify the effective gain in the motor system, and thus MBON valence would also be sensitive to activation timing.
evidence: This is an inference from the proposed model.

claim: It should not be possible to yield a change in odour attraction behaviour via optogenetic activation of a target MBON unless the stimulus respects the timing sensitivity of the larval oscillator.
source: That is, it should not be possible to yield a change in odour attraction behaviour via optogenetic activation of a target MBON unless the stimulus respects the timing sensitivity of the larval oscillator, mimicking a closed-loop motor action-stimulation.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: The modularity of the proposed system could provide evolutionary flexibility since it allows for behaviour to adapt by simply plugging in or removing input modalities.
source: The modularity of the system described here could provide such an evolutionary flexibility since it allows for behaviour to adapt by simply plugging in or removing input modalities.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about evolutionary implications.

claim: Over long time scales, natural selection favours not merely effective innovations, but systems that flexibly enable the incorporation of innovations.
source: It has been argued that over long time scales, natural selection favours not merely effective innovations, but systems that flexibly enable the incorporation of innovations (Vermeij, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: Each 3rd-instar foraging-larva path was recorded for 5 min at 7fps.
source: Each 3rd-instar foraging-larva path was recorded for 5 min at 7fps after releasing each larva on a rectangular agarose slab opposite to an odour source given by an ethyl butyrate droplet suspended from the lid.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used to collect the data.

claim: Body bending was calculated as the angle formed between the tail-to-centroid axis and centroid-to-head axis.
source: Body bending was calculated as the angle formed between the tail-to-centroid axis and centroid-to-head axis.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method.

claim: The variable 'angular velocity of the anterior part of the body' was obtained as the derivative across time of the centroid-to-head axis orientation.
source: The variable 'angular velocity of the anterior part of the body' was obtained as the derivative across time of the centroid-to-head axis orientation.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method.
